docs.title: iam-blast-radius
docs.text:
IAM findings get triaged by severity label. The question that decides whether a compromise is contained is a different one: if this principal is taken, what is reachable, and in how many steps.

This computes that. It reads an account snapshot, builds a privilege reachability graph from the escalation primitives that actually grant one principal another's permissions, and reports which principals reach administrative access, by which route, and at what hop distance.

The headline it produces is the gap between intention and fact: the share of principals somebody labelled least privilege that reach admin anyway.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• The escalation edges is the list the tool's correctness rests on, with the rationale for each.
  • Preparing a real account covers the export and what to strip from it.
  • The example report is regenerated on every docs deploy from a synthetic account.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
As a container, which is the distribution channel for this project:

docker pull ghcr.io/__GITHUB_USERNAME__/iam-blast-radius:latest

Or from source:

pip install git+https://github.com/__GITHUB_USERNAME__/iam-blast-radius.git

docs.title: The shortest useful run
docs.text:
ibr generate --principals 2000 --out account.json --seed 7
ibr analyse --account account.json --out report.html

The first command exists so the tool can be evaluated without exporting anything real. Replace it with a snapshot of your own account and the numbers stop being a simulation.

docs.title: What it never does
docs.text: No AWS calls, no credentials, no writes. The account is a file, and the analysis path has no network code in it at all. That is a design decision with a reason, recorded in ADR-001: a service that could refresh itself from AWS would need a role with iam:List* across the account, and that role is a more attractive target than the report it produces.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• ADR-001: an offline graph rather than the IAM policy simulator.
  • ADR-002: one traversal rather than a search per principal, and the 118 seconds that forced it.
  • ADR-003: why every approximation errs toward reporting more reachability, and the one place it does not.

docs.title: The escalation edges
docs.text:
A node is a principal. An edge from A to B means a compromise of A yields B's privileges. This page is the list, because the tool is only as correct as it is: a missing edge is a principal reported contained when it is not, which is worse than not running the tool at all because it manufactures confidence.

The techniques are the documented AWS privilege escalation families. The implementation and the preconditions are this project's own.

docs.title: The edges
docs.text: Edge Required actions What an attacker does assume_role sts:AssumeRole Assume the target role directly attach_policy iam:AttachUserPolicy Attach AdministratorAccess to yourself put_inline_policy iam:PutUserPolicy Write yourself an inline policy granting any action create_access_key iam:CreateAccessKey Create long lived credentials for another user update_login_profile iam:UpdateLoginProfile Set a console password for another user pass_role_to_lambda iam:PassRole, lambda:CreateFunction, lambda:InvokeFunction Run code as the target role pass_role_to_ec2 iam:PassRole, ec2:RunInstances Launch an instance with the target role attached update_assume_role_policy iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy, sts:AssumeRole Rewrite the trust policy to name yourself, then assume add_user_to_group iam:AddUserToGroup Add yourself to a more privileged group

docs.title: The preconditions that matter
docs.text:
An edge is not created just because the source holds the actions. Three checks remove paths that would fail at the first API call, and each of them was a bug before it was a check.

sts:AssumeRole means nothing without the trust policy. Holding the action in an identity policy is half the requirement; the target role's trust policy has to name the principal. Skipping this turns every principal with sts:AssumeRole into a path to every role in the account, which is the single most common way a reachability tool produces a report nobody believes.

Passing a role to a service requires the service to trust it. A role that does not trust lambda.amazonaws.com cannot back a function, so iam:PassRole plus lambda:CreateFunction against it is not a path. The first version of this tool created those edges and they were all false.

Resource scope is evaluated. A principal allowed iam:CreateAccessKey only on its own ARN reaches nobody. These look alarming in a policy grep and are not findings, which is why the bundled account contains them deliberately: the resource scoping needs something to get right.

docs.title: What is not an edge
docs.text:
Rolling a policy back to an older version. iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion is a real escalation primitive and it is not an edge, because an edge means "A obtains B's privileges" and here there is no B: the principal gains more of its own permissions. It is evaluated as admin equivalence instead, and only when a non default version actually grants an administrative action. Modelling it as an edge produced a path from the principal to everyone whose policy had any old version, including rollbacks that granted nothing but s3:List*.

Anything an administrator can do. An administrator reaches every principal by definition. Those edges are not stored: "the administrator can attach a policy to this user" is not a finding, and enumerating them added hundreds of thousands of entries nobody acts on. Blast radius for an administrator is the account.

docs.title: Admin equivalence
docs.text:
A principal is treated as already administrative when it can perform any of a set of concrete API actions that grant arbitrary privilege: iam:AttachUserPolicy, iam:PutUserPolicy, iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:PutRolePolicy, iam:AttachGroupPolicy, iam:PutGroupPolicy, iam:CreatePolicyVersion.

Every entry is a concrete action and never a wildcard, which is less obvious than it sounds. An earlier version included the literal strings * and iam:*. Asking whether a principal is allowed the action * matches an Allow on * while an explicit Deny on iam:* does not match it, because * is not an action anybody can call. PowerUserAccess, which is exactly Allow * plus Deny iam:*, was therefore reported as administrative.

docs.title: Adding one
docs.text: See CONTRIBUTING. The short version: state the actions, the technique, and why holding them grants the target's privileges rather than merely touching it, and write a test for both halves, that the edge appears when it should and that it does not when a precondition is missing. The second half is what catches an edge that reaches everybody.

docs.title: Preparing a real account
docs.text: The tool reads a JSON snapshot. The bundled generator exists so it can be evaluated without one; this page is how to produce the real thing.

docs.title: The export
docs.text:
Everything needed comes from one call:

aws iam get-account-authorization-details \
  --filter User Role Group LocalManagedPolicy AWSManagedPolicy \
  > raw.json

That requires iam:GetAccountAuthorizationDetails, which is read only. The tool itself never makes this call and never holds the credential that can: see ADR-001 for why that boundary is where it is.

docs.title: The transform
docs.text:
The snapshot format is documented by src/ibr/account/serialise.py and is deliberately small. For each principal you need:

  • principal_id and principal_type
  • inline_statements: effect, actions, resources, and the names of any condition keys
  • attached_policy_arns
  • group_ids for users
  • trust_policy for roles: trusted principals, trusted services, condition key names
  • tags

For each managed policy you need every version, with is_default marked on one. The versions matter: rolling back to an older one is an escalation primitive and a snapshot carrying only the default version cannot detect it.

docs.title: What to strip
docs.text:
Condition key values. The model records that a statement is conditional and the names of the keys. It never evaluates them and never needs their values, and values frequently carry account ids, VPC ids and IP ranges.

Resource ARNs that are not principals. The tool matches resource patterns against principal identifiers. An S3 bucket ARN in a statement is noise to it and may be sensitive to you.

Policy descriptions and tags you do not want in a report. Tags are carried into the output, which is how the least privilege label is read. Strip any tag you would not want in a ticket.

docs.title: Handling the output
docs.text: Treat the snapshot and the report the way you treat the account. Both name principals and the escalation paths between them, and the report is a shorter, better organised version of the attack plan. SECURITY.md has the full argument.

docs.title: Multi account
docs.text:
Out of scope for v1, and worth being precise about why. Cross account escalation runs through role trust policies naming external principals, which the model records but cannot resolve without the other account's snapshot. Until it can, a role trusting an external principal is a boundary the tool reports and does not follow.

The honest consequence: in an organisation, a single account analysis understates reachability. If you run this per account, read the trust policies naming external principals as open edges rather than closed ones.

docs.title: ADR-001: An offline reachability graph rather than the IAM policy simulator
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
AWS ships an authoritative answer to "can this principal perform this action": iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy. It evaluates the real policy language including condition keys, permission boundaries and service control policies, which is more than this project implements and always will be.

The question this tool asks is not that one. It asks: given every principal in an account, which of them can obtain administrative privileges, by what route, and in how many steps. That is a transitive question over tens of thousands of pairs, and the simulator answers one pair at a time.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Call the simulator for every pair. Rejected on arithmetic before anything else. A 20,000 principal account has 400 million ordered pairs, and even restricted to plausible ones the call count is in the millions at a request rate measured in tens per second. It would also require credentials with iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy across the account, and it would put the audit's load on the production IAM control plane.
  2. Call the simulator to confirm each edge the graph finds. Attractive, and still rejected for v1: it reintroduces the credential requirement and the rate limit for the subset of pairs that matter, and the pairs that matter are exactly the ones an attacker would be probing. Recorded in the roadmap as an opt in verification pass rather than the default.
  3. Parse policies offline and build a reachability graph. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Model the subset of IAM that determines whether one principal can obtain another's privileges, build a directed graph from it, and answer reachability questions by traversal. No AWS calls in the analysis path at all.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The tool runs with no credentials, no account access and no network, which is what lets the entire test suite execute on a clean checkout and lets the service run anywhere. That is not a convenience: a service that could refresh itself from AWS would need a role with iam:List* and iam:Get* across the account, which is a more attractive thing to compromise than the report it produces.

The cost is real and is stated rather than hidden. Condition keys are recorded and not evaluated. Permission boundaries and service control policies are recorded and not applied. Resource policies other than role trust are out of scope. Each of those can only make the real answer more restrictive than the reported one, which is the direction ADR-003 argues for deliberately.

The subset is small enough to be read in one sitting, which matters more than it sounds. The correctness of this tool rests on src/ibr/graph/edges.py being complete and src/ibr/account/model.py being right about Deny, and both are short enough for a reviewer to check rather than trust.

docs.title: ADR-002: One traversal, not a search per principal
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The first working version of this tool was correct and unusable. On a 2,177 principal account it took 118 seconds to build the graph and a further 35 seconds to answer the reachability question, which is not a tool anybody runs weekly.

Three separate mistakes, each the obvious implementation of its step.

Edge construction tested every pair. Every principal against every principal, for every escalation definition, with a full policy evaluation inside the innermost loop. Quadratic in principals with an expensive constant.

Effective statements were recomputed every time. Resolving what a principal is allowed walks its inline statements, its attached managed policies and every group it belongs to. The build asked for the same principal's statements thousands of times and recomputed from scratch each time.

Reachability enumerated simple paths per principal. all_simple_paths from every principal to every administrative node. With 338 administrative nodes in that account, that is 2,177 searches against 338 targets each, to extract two numbers: the hop distance and one shortest path.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Memoise effective statements on the Account. Index candidate targets from the resource patterns a principal is actually allowed the escalation action on. Replace per principal path enumeration with a single breadth first search over the reversed graph, seeded with every administrative node.

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
On a 2,177 principal account, median of three runs:

Stage Before After Graph build 118 s 1.5 s Reachability 34.9 s 0.016 s

The reachability change is the larger one and the more interesting. A reverse breadth first search labels every principal with its distance to the nearest administrative node in one pass, linear in the graph. Recording the first step of each shortest path during that pass means the path is reconstructed by following pointers rather than searched for again.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Candidate indexing changes the shape of the work, not just its speed. A principal allowed iam:CreateAccessKey only on its own ARN has exactly one candidate. A principal holding no escalation action at all has none, and the majority of principals in any account hold none. Only a principal with a wildcard resource scope expands to the whole account, and that principal is itself the finding.

Administrative principals are skipped as edge sources. An administrator reaches every principal by definition, and enumerating those edges added hundreds of thousands of entries that nobody acts on: "the administrator can attach a policy to this user" is not a finding. Blast radius for an administrator is reported as the whole account by the query layer rather than stored as edges.

The count of enumerated paths was replaced. It was exponential to compute and told a reader nothing they acted on. What replaced it is the number of distinct next steps that lead toward admin, which is the out degree restricted to neighbours closer to admin: how many separate statements have to be removed to contain this principal. Cheaper and more useful.

Blast radius per principal is off by default. It is a breadth first search per principal, which is quadratic over the account, while every other number here comes from one traversal. The CLI computes it only for the principals it displays, and the API computes it per request, which is the right shape for a question asked about one principal at a time.

The remaining ceiling is edge count rather than principal count. An account where many principals hold wildcard scoped IAM write actions produces millions of edges, and that is a true property of the account rather than an artefact: the graph is large because the blast radius is large.

docs.title: ADR-003: Over report reachability rather than under report it
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-20

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Several places in this tool face the same choice: an edge might exist, and the evaluator cannot be certain.

A statement allows iam:PassRole but carries a condition key the model records and does not evaluate. A permission boundary is attached and not applied. A service control policy exists above the account and is not read.

In each case the tool can include the edge and flag it, or exclude it.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Exclude anything uncertain. Produces a clean report with no false positives and an unknown number of false negatives. Every excluded edge is a path the report says does not exist.
  2. Include everything uncertain, unflagged. Produces a report nobody trusts after the first time an engineer chases a path that a condition blocks.
  3. Include and flag, with an option to exclude. Chosen.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Include the edge, mark it conditional, and surface that in every output. The report shows which principals reach admin only through a conditional edge. --strict-conditions and IBR_ASSUME_CONDITIONS=false flip the behaviour for anybody who wants the conservative set.

docs.title: The argument, stated plainly
docs.text:
The two errors are not symmetric and treating them as a tuning problem misses the point.

A false positive costs an engineer the time to check one path. They open the policy, see the condition, confirm it holds, and move on. Ten minutes, and the tool is slightly less pleasant to use.

A false negative costs a breach. The report said the principal was contained. Nobody looked again.

Every approximation in this tool is therefore pushed in the same direction: toward reporting more reachability than certainly exists. Conditions are assumed satisfiable. Permission boundaries are not applied, which can only make the real answer more restrictive. Trust policy conditions are flagged rather than evaluated.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The report has to say this, and it does: the footer of the HTML output states what was not evaluated, and the conditional count is one of the four headline tiles rather than a footnote. A tool that over reports without saying so is simply a tool that is wrong.

The flag matters for the people who need the other direction. A team doing quarterly attestation rather than incident response may want the set they can defend as certain, and --strict-conditions gives it to them with the trade stated.

The one place this reasoning does not apply is explicit Deny, which is evaluated properly and always wins. A Deny is not an uncertainty: it is a fact in the policy that makes the edge not exist, and including it anyway would be reporting a path that provably cannot be taken. The asymmetry argument is about things the evaluator does not know, not about things it does.

docs.title: Forensics audit: iam-blast-radius at v0.3.0
docs.text: Four personas, each auditing independently, then an integrated verdict. Graded PASS, WEAK or FAIL. Every FAIL found during this audit was fixed with its own commit before delivery.

docs.title: Persona 1: The Principal Engineer
docs.text: # Question Grade Justification 1 Clone, run, verify PASS Tested in a clean directory from the README text alone. make verify runs the same checks as CI in the same order, through an explicit interpreter rather than through console scripts that bind to whichever Python installed them. No AWS account, no credentials, no network. 2 Architecture and design decisions PASS Four packages with a real boundary each: account models and serialises, graph builds and traverses, api serves, report renders. The split that matters is between edge construction and traversal, which is why the performance work changed both independently without touching the model. Three ADRs, each with rejected options and measurements. 3 Abstraction and configurability PASS Hop limits, path caps, condition handling and the seed all on Config from the environment with validation. --strict-conditions exposes the one approximation a user might reasonably want reversed. 4 Error handling and edge cases PASS Eleven documented failure modes. The account loader refuses an unsupported schema version rather than misreading it, because a silently misread account is a confidently wrong report. Group cycles are guarded, which matters because the model is loaded from a file that could contain one. 5 Testing PASS 155 tests, 98 percent branch coverage, including a regression test for each of the three modelling bugs and structural tests on the Dockerfile. The convention that each edge needs two tests, one that it appears and one that it does not when a precondition is missing, came out of the war story rather than being imposed.

docs.title: Persona 2: The UX Director and Product Thinker
docs.text: # Question Grade Justification 1 First 30 seconds PASS Opens with the gap between a label and a fact, and the number measuring it. Not a technology, not a feature list. 2 The So What of results PASS Every finding carries the principals it passes through and the technique at each step. The report's own framing is that a number tells somebody there is a problem and a path tells them which statement to delete. 3 Visual storytelling PASS The architecture diagram shows that no AWS call appears anywhere in the pipeline, which is the design's main claim. The report leads with one figure, carries status by glyph and word as well as colour, and states what it did not evaluate in the footer rather than burying it. 4 Actionability and handoff PASS Four CLI verbs covering generate, analyse, gate and serve, so the tool fits a review, a CI check and an incident without reconfiguration. Future Work names the first metric to watch and explains why the obvious one is wrong.

docs.title: Persona 3: The Hiring Manager
docs.text: # Question Grade Justification 1 Tutorial smell test PASS The problem is specific and current: severity labels do not answer a transitive question, and the path runs through three principals so no single policy document contains it. 2 Stolen Valor check PASS after a fix Was a FAIL. duckdb and pyyaml were declared and never imported. Removed, and the CloudTrail activity scan duckdb was there for is recorded as out of scope with a trigger condition rather than left as an implied capability. The tech stack table now distinguishes what networkx provides from what this project does with it. 3 Hardest problem solved PASS Three bugs that are the same bug: each modelled one side of a two sided relationship. The writeup draws that out rather than listing them, and the test convention that came from it is in CONTRIBUTING. 4 One thing I will remember PASS That PowerUserAccess was reported as an administrator because the admin set contained the literal string *, which is not an action anybody can call, so the Allow matched and the Deny did not.

docs.title: Persona 4: The Sceptic (provenance)
docs.text:
Automated by scripts/provenance_check.py.

The FAILs found and fixed during this audit:

  1. Two declared dependencies nothing imported. Fixed, and tools/check_dependencies.py now fails CI on the class. This is the third repository in the batch where that check has caught something.
  2. The benchmark's largest scenario did not complete, so the published scaling claim rested on two points. Rather than quietly benchmarking smaller, the ceiling was measured directly and the README now carries the edge growth table, the memory figure and the wall clock limit.

The remaining WEAKs, each with a reason:

  • Identity placeholders unresolved. Expected: built before the GitHub account was known. tools/set_identity.sh binds every URL in one pass.
  • The image is not built in this environment. Docker Hub is unreachable from the development sandbox, so the image is built, run and health checked in CI instead, and tests/test_dockerfile.py asserts the file still says what the README and SECURITY.md claim it says. This is stated rather than papered over: no image size or runtime behaviour is published from an unbuilt image.

docs.title: Integrated verdict
docs.text:
Overall portfolio score: 9 out of 10.

The repository holds up to all four reads. Its strongest feature is that the correctness surface is small and explicit: the tool is exactly as good as src/ibr/graph/edges.py and src/ibr/account/model.py, both are short enough for a reviewer to read rather than trust, and the README says so.

The performance work is the clearest engineering in the batch so far, because all three mistakes were the obvious implementation of their step and the fixes are measured rather than asserted: 118 seconds to 1.5 on graph construction, 34.9 to 0.016 on reachability.

It is a 9 and not a 10 because it has not been pushed: the Actions tab is not green, the releases are local tags, and the image is publish ready rather than published. For this repository that gap is larger than for the others, because the image is the distribution channel and an unpublished image is an untested one beyond what the structural tests cover.

docs.title: Critical failures (do not ship)
docs.text: None outstanding.

docs.title: Impact multipliers
docs.text:
1. Push and publish. Green Actions tab, three GitHub Releases from the existing annotated tags, the image on ghcr.io with its provenance attestation, and Pages live so the badge endpoints resolve. The image job in CI already builds, runs and health checks it; it has simply never run.
  2. Verify against the policy simulator. Issue 03. It is the only way to measure this tool's false positive rate against the authority rather than against its own fixtures, and given that three modelling bugs were found by hand, the rate is the number a sceptical reader most wants.
  3. Multi account. Issue 01. A single account analysis understates reachability in an organisation, which the README states, and stating a limitation is not the same as removing it.

docs.title: Elevator pitch
docs.text: IAM findings get triaged by severity label, but the question that decides whether a compromise is contained is transitive: can this principal reach administrative access, and how far does it have to go. Nobody answers that by reading policies, because the path runs through three principals and no single policy document contains it. This builds the privilege reachability graph from nine documented escalation primitives, reports which principals reach admin and by which route, and ships as a container that holds no credentials and makes no AWS calls. On the bundled account, roughly a quarter of the principals somebody tagged least privilege reach administrative access anyway.
